items.title: Oilers thwarted by rookie Red Wings goalie as depth salvages point
items.summary: The Oilers’ young guys looked pretty good, but the one between the pipes for the Red Wings looked better.
items.body: EDMONTON — If you came away with anything from the Edmonton Oilers ’ 4-3 shootout loss to the Detroit Red Wings Monday night, it was that the young guys looked pretty good. The only problem was, the young guy who looked the best was 24-year-old Michal Postava, the goaltender making his first National Hockey League start in the Red Wings’ net. “He’s solid,” said Ryan Nugent-Hopkins , the third Oiler to be thwarted by Postava in the shootout, allowing Lucas Raymond’s wrist shot past Tristan Jarry to stand up as the game-winner. “I thought he was good positionally and always there. Even in the shootout, I saw both Connor and Leo deke, and he stuck with it. I tried to beat him with a shot and he was right there.” Postava was better than excellent, robbing Evan Bouchard twice in overtime, then stopping each of Connor McDavid , Leon Draisaitl and Nugent-Hopkins in the shootout. He’s an undrafted rookie from a Czech town of 25,000, who the Oilers had interest in when he chose Detroit. You never know with goalies — whether he goes on to greatness or becomes a one-game wonder — but if nothing else Postava will have a heck of a tale to tell the grandchildren one day. “It’s amazing, I feel like a kid,” he beamed post-game. “I watched all those NHL games when I was young and I didn’t expect to one day be in the net and win the game. Now, I’m just so happy.” It was a pretty nice debut, putting a shootout “X” beside the names of two of hockey’s best shooters — Nos. 97 and 29. “It’s crazy,” he said. “You look at how many points they have so far — they’re two of the best players in the world right now. items.title: Youngsters set tone for Flames in ‘Griddy’ win
items.summary: They didn’t name the dance after him, but if he continues to grow his game like he has as of late, Matvei Gridin may very well be remembered for it.
items.body: CALGARY — They didn’t name the dance after him, but if he continues to grow his game like he has of late, Matvei Gridin may very well be remembered for it. Seven years after a high school touchdown celebration known as The Griddy went viral, Gridin punctuated his second goal in Monday night’s 5-2 win over the Leafs with an icy version of the TikTok staple. “Obviously my nickname is Griddy, and I was thinking about that for a long time, and I thought it was a good moment to do that — up by three and having fun,” said the Flames’ 20-year-old winger of a groove that sees the performer alternately tap their heels while swinging their arms. “A couple old guys said it was a bit too much, but I think they loved it.” Smart money says he’ll have plenty of opportunities he’s sure to make good on to perfect the move. After all, the uber-confident Russian first-rounder was the one who declared last spring he'd lead the team in scoring this year. “I didn’t see it coming — I kind of backed up and let him do it,” beamed Zayne Parekh , who set up the filthy roof job over Sergei Bobrovsky’s glove with a 150-foot pass out of his zone just 25 seconds into the second period. “I told him before the draw to be ready and all I saw was his stick touching the ceiling, and he wanted that thing. What a shot. Special. He’s going to score a lot of goals in this league and I’m not surprised he scored from there.” There, meaning just a few strides into the Leafs zone on the left wing with a rocket far-side. “There’s no ill thought in his head, he’s just a kid having fun, and we’re having fun as a team right now,” said Parekh. items.title: Maple Leafs’ Auston Matthews unhappy with delay-of-game penalty
items.body: Toronto Maple Leafs captain Auston Matthews is pushing back on the third-period penalty called against him in Monday's loss to the Calgary Flames. Matthews was called for delay-of-game midway through the final frame with his Maple Leafs trailing by one goal — the seventh penalty assessed to Toronto and negating a power play that had only just begun for the Maple Leafs. On-ice officials determined that the 29-year-old played the puck with his glove following a faceoff, which results in a delay-of-game penalty per NHL Rule 67.2. "I think you've got to be sure 100 per cent," he said to reporters after the game in Calgary. "I fall. I don't even know what exactly the rule is, if you have to cover it or whatever, but I've got a lot of respect for the refs. They're going to make what they feel is the right call. They're not perfect, but obviously in that situation, I feel like you really gotta be sure." Matthews said he wasn't given an explanation after his penalty. The official rule states that a player shall be assessed a minor penalty if he attempts to win a face-off by batting the puck with his hands. The two players involved in the actual face-off (the centres) are not permitted to play the puck with their hand without incurring a penalty under this rule until such time as a third player (from either team) has at least touched the puck. Once the face-off is deemed complete (and a winner of the face-off is clear) hand passes shall be enforced as per Rule 79 – Hand Pass. Head coach Jim Hiller told reporters post-game that the referees explained that the puck hit Matthews' glove, and that's why he was assessed the penalty. items.title: Cowan tries taking blame for Maple Leafs loss
items.body: CALGARY — The second-youngest Toronto Maple Leaf was the first one standing in the middle of the Saddledome visitors' room, ready to assume all the blame. "Bad turnover and dumb penalty by me. So, those two goals are on me, and I got to be better. Cost us the game," Easton Cowan said Monday night, swallowing Toronto’s streak-snapping loss to the Calgary Flames whole. Cowan’s own-zone turnover in the first period led directly to a Mikael Backlund goal, then his overaggressive double minor for roughing at the end of the frame resulted in a Matvei Gridin power-play winner. Gridin hit the griddy, and the red-hot, house-money home team built enough of a cushion to dance its way to a 5-2 victory (with a couple empty netters). Cowan, whose praises had been sung by GM John Chayka mere hours before puck drop, admitted that frustration over his early turnover bled into his unnecessary infraction. “Yeah, it was selfish of me to take that dumb penalty. Can't have that. Got to be better. Got to control my emotions better,” he said. "Just got to be better, have better character." items.title: Raymond completes Red Wings’ rally with shootout winner over Oilers
items.body: Lucas Raymond scored the shootout winner and had a pair of assists in regulation time as the Detroit Red Wings posted a 4-3 victory over the Edmonton Oilers on Monday. Viktor Arvidsson, Emmitt Finnie and Dylan Larkin scored in regulation for the Red Wings (5-4-3) who went 2-1-1 on their Northwestern road trip. Michal Postava made 25 stops and added three more in the shootout session to earn the win in Detroit's net. Vasily Podkolzin, Isaac Howard and Colton Dach replied for the Oilers (8-2-2), who have lost two straight as well as forward Zach Hyman to what looked to be a concussion. Red Wings: Postava made his first NHL start. The 24-year-old undrafted netminder from Czechia was actually appearing in his second career game, replacing John Gibson in the third period of a 5-2 win against Vancouver last Thursday. Oilers: Connor McDavid extended his season-starting points streak to 12 games, now with a staggering 34 points in that span. He set a new Oilers record for most points before Nov. 1, and also matched the longest season-opening assist streak in NHL history, equalling Sebastian Aho, Ken Linseman and Wayne Gretzky. Detroit tied the game for a third time with just 1:17 remaining in the third and their goalie pulled as a bouncing puck came to Larkin in front and he shovelled in just his second of the season to send the game to extra time. The Oilers came into the game with a fair amount of recent success against Detroit, going 6-1-2 in their last nine overall and 4-0-2 in their last six home meetings.

items.title: Kochetkov just thinking 'about hockey' during perfect start for Hurricanes
items.summary: Pyotr Kochetkov said he's in a better state of mind this season after battling back from a lower-body injury, and it shows in his play.
items.body: Pyotr Kochetkov said he's in a better state of mind this season after battling back from a lower-body injury, and it shows in his play. The Carolina Hurricanes goalie is off to a 7-0-0 start and can maintain his perfect record when the defending Stanley Cup champions host the Boston Bruins at Lenovo Center on Tuesday (8 p.m. ET; ESPN, SN360). "I'm happy to be playing because I only played nine games last season and that was tough mentally," Kochetkov said last week in Edmonton. "But it was actually good to see a game from the outside and it teaches you. Now when I have a bad night, I just think about how it's better to have a bad night than to not be playing at all. "I'm happy that I'm on this team and I'm happy I'm able to play. I don't think about too many other things now, I just think about hockey." CAR@STL: Kochetkov makes 24 saves for first shutout of season Overcoming the injury has given Kochetkov a new appreciation for the game and he's made the most of his seven starts this season. The 27-year-old has a 1.70 goals-against average and .916 save percentage. He made 24 saves in a 4-0 win at the St. Louis Blues on Saturday for his first shutout of the season and 12th in the NHL. "I'm happy for him, it's hard to come back after missing that many games," Carolina defenseman Jalen Chatfield said. "He's a workhorse, he puts in a lot of work, and I know he wants it. I played with him with the Chicago Wolves (in the American Hockey League) five or six years ago, so I've seen firsthand how he's developed and the way he takes care of his body. "Injuries are going to happen. It's the way you bounce back from that and the way he's done it so far, credit to him because he had put in the work." items.title: Auston Matthews becomes fastest in Maple Leafs history to reach 800 points
items.body: Auston Matthews keeps adding his name to the Toronto Maple Leafs record book. With an assist on William Nylander's third-period goal on Monday, the captain became the fastest player in franchise history to reach the 800-point milestone, doing so in just 703 games. He surpassed previous record-holder Darryl Sittler, who hit 800 in 742 games in 1980. The 2022 league MVP is off to another hot start, with nine goals and 11 assists in 14 games. Matthews has produced at a point-per-game clip in all but two seasons in his 10-year career. His most productive season came in 2023-24, when he scored 69 goals and registered 107 points en route to his third Rocket Richard Trophy. Though the Maple Leafs lost Monday's game, Toronto still sits third in the Atlantic Division with a 7-5-2 record.

items.body: Add to Preferred Sources The Toronto Maple Leafs confirmed Monday evening that winger Kirill Marchenko sustained a lower-body injury during the second period of their game against the Calgary Flames at the Scotiabank Saddledome. Marchenko, 26, fell awkwardly into the boards in the Leafs’ attacking zone after being hit by Flames forward Yegor Sharangovich. The 6’3″ right wing left the ice in clear discomfort and quickly went down the tunnel towards the Leafs’ dressing room. The Barnaul, Russia product has been a fixture on Toronto’s No. 1 power-play unit, as well as on a line with William Nylander during 5-on-5 play. The Blue Jackets originally selected Marchenko in the second round (No. 49 overall) of the 2018 NHL Draft. After emerging as a top KHL player with SKA St. Petersburg, Marchenko came to North America with the Blue Jackets organization in 2022. But on the eve of what would’ve been his fifth season in Columbus, Marchenko was traded to the Leafs alongside Miles Wood and Elvis Merzlikins in exchange for a package headlined by Matthew Knies. items.title: Kings continue hot Eastern Conference trip with win over Rangers
items.summary: Drew Doughty had a goal and two assists, and Artemi Panarin added a power-play goal and an assist as the Los Angeles Kings beat the New York Rangers 6-3 on Monday night.
items.body: NEW YORK — Drew Doughty had a goal and two assists, and Artemi Panarin added a power-play goal and an assist as the Los Angeles Kings beat the New York Rangers 6-3 on Monday night. The Kings won for the third time in their last four games — all on the road — after going winless over their first six games of the season. Los Angeles jumped on New York early, chasing goaltender James Reimer after one period. Reimer was pulled in his Rangers debut after allowing three goals on eight shots. Reimer played just one previous game this fall, a 35-save shutout in the American Hockey League on Saturday night, before signing an NHL contract for the rest of the season. Taylor Ward opened the scoring 1:15 into the game on the Kings’ first shot. Brandt Clarke made it 2-0 at 4:52 of the first, tipping in a rebound off Joel Armia's slap shot. J.T. Miller got New York on the board when a Tye Kartye slap shot deflected off his skate and past Darcy Kuemper. Mikey Anderson and Taylor Ward added second-period goals for the Kings before Adam Fox cut the deficit to 5-2 on the power play with 6:55 to play in the second. Kartye got the Rangers within two at 16:08 of the third period, before Joel Edmundson scored in an empty net for his first goal of the season for Los Angeles. Kuemper made 23 saves to pick up his third win of the season. After replacing Reimer, Dylan Garand stopped 15 of the 17 shots he faced. A moment of silence was held prior to puck drop for 1970s and ’80s Rangers fan favourite Ron Duguay, who died last week.

Doughty has seen longtime teammates and peers retire and this, his 19th NHL season, is the final season of his eight-year, $88 million contract ($11 million average annual value). items.title: Jets get welcome distraction from Heritage Classic, look for on-ice reset
items.summary: Winnipeg’s Heritage Classic delivered a much-needed celebration of the franchise’s history and following Connor Hellebuyck’s departure, the Jets look to turn the page and put the focus on turning things around on the ice.
items.body: By almost every account, the NHL's Heritage Classic festivities were a smashing success. The Jets couldn't quite tie the bow on the weekend, falling 2-1 to the Montreal Canadiens in front of a sold-out crowd at Princess Auto Stadium. But everything from the fan festival to a heavy dose of nostalgia at the alumni game, to the marquee event on a beautifully sunny Sunday was executed with passion and style, generating incredible energy from start to finish. "Myself personally, I told my grandkids to be ready for the (military) flyover (before the game) and I'm sure that's all they're going to talk about is the jets and the helicopters," head coach Scott Arniel said of the atmosphere. "To be in a Canadian market, two Canadian teams like that, that's special." Jets captain Adam Lowry was equally appreciative of the moment, both for Winnipeg and the greater hockey community. "It was a spectacular spectacle," Lowry said. "It takes you back to youth hockey, it takes you back to growing up when you fell in love with the game." Beneath all the cheers and nostalgia, however, the Heritage Classic served as the perfect distraction from the circus that had been playing out in Winnipeg ever since franchise goaltender Connor Hellebuyck publicly demanded a trade in August. items.body: NEWARK, N.J. – Sheldon Keefe and his New Jersey Devils’ staff added it all up. Since the start of training camp in September, Connor Hellebuyck spent 29 days on the ice honing his game in Michigan against NHL shooters like Robby Fabbri, which is one more than his new tandem mate, Jake Allen, worked with the Devils. In other words: There will be no long ramp-up to game shape required for Hellebuyck. And that’s exactly how the best goaltender of his generation wants it – to be thrown right into the fire. But if you’re asking me, I am.” Hellebuyck said he spent Sunday’s off day, his first day of rest in weeks, house hunting and familiarizing himself with the North Jersey area. He undoubtedly scouted a fishing spot or two with intel from a former teammate. And his first Devils mask is in the process of being painted. items.body: Register Login Golden Knights Recall Jonas Rondbjerg; Reassign Alexander Holtz By Brennan McClain | at October 26, 2026 2:30 pm According to a team announcement , the Vegas Golden Knights have recalled forward Jonas Røndbjerg from the AHL’s Henderson Silver Knights. In a corresponding roster move, the Golden Knights reassigned forward Alexander Holtz . Røndbjerg, 27, has been a frequent call-up by the Golden Knights for the past few years, particularly when the team runs into injury trouble. With winger Victor Olofsson out for the foreseeable future with an upper-body injury, Vegas has had to lean on its forward depth. Still, the Golden Knights haven’t yet used Røndbjerg this season. His most recent NHL playing time came last season, when he registered one assist in four games for Vegas while averaging 12:05 of ice time per game. Throughout his career, Røndbjerg has scored three goals and 11 points in 80 games, all with the Golden Knights. The Rungsted, Denmark, native has understandably performed better with AHL Henderson. A reliable tertiary scorer, Røndbjerg has registered 65 goals and 147 points in 283 AHL contests with a +15 rating. This season, Røndbjerg has tallied two assists in seven games. Despite the call-up, Røndbjerg is unlikely to play unless the Golden Knights sustain another forward injury. Meanwhile, Holtz returns to the AHL after two games with Vegas. Filling in for Mitch Marner , who was out for the birth of his child, Holtz registered one assist in two games with a -1 rating, averaging 11:47 of ice time per game. He’ll look to continue his torrid start with AHL Henderson, where he scored four goals and eight points in five games.

The watch list breaks prospects into distinct tiers: A (projected first-rounder), B (second-to-third-rounder), C (fourth-to-fifth-rounder), and W (sixth-to-seventh-rounder). items.title: Hurricanes GM Eric Tulsky talks about why Alexander Nikishin’s contract extension took so long
items.summary: Nikishin’s absence from the Hurricanes ended Sunday with a one-year, $3 million contract.
items.body: Add to Preferred Sources Credit: James Guillory-Imagn Images Looming contract and trade situations have been getting resolved en masse throughout the NHL in the past couple of weeks, including one involving the reigning Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes . On Sunday, defenseman Alexander Nikishin ended his holdout by signing a one-year, $3 million contract that will walk him to a version of restricted free agency where he would be eligible to sign an offer sheet and would have arbitration rights. Nikishin had neither of those options this year, limiting his leverage even as he requested a trade away from the Hurricanes. The Hurricanes reportedly attempted to use Nikishin as a trade chip to land star goalie Connor Hellebuyck, who was ultimately dealt to the New Jersey Devils last Friday. On Monday’s episode of The Sheet , hosts Jeff Marek and Greg Wyshynski were joined by Hurricanes general manager Eric Tulsky to discuss the resolution of Nikishin’s contract situation. Jeff Marek: “One of the questions that everyone’s asking: why did it take until late October? Eric Tulsky: “Sometimes it takes time to work through a process. We had a lot of different things we were looking at. We had to work through it, had to sort of get to a place that everyone was comfortable with. And that happens at a different pace in different negotiations.” Jeff Marek: “What was it? But was an agent change a factor that sort of paused things? Does that ever significantly pause things? Eric Tulsky : “You definitely have a little bit of a reset when there’s the change because the new agent needs to get up to speed on the file and talk to everybody and make sure he understands the position. And so that means you’ve got a little bit more work to do. Iit’s a little bit of a reason for the delay.

items.body: Edmonton Oilers centre Leon Draisaitl, Calgary Flames goaltender Devin Cooley and Montreal Canadiens goaltender Jacob Fowler have been named the NHL's three stars of the week. Draisaitl scored a league-best six goals and added three assists over three games as the Oilers won twice and moved into first place in the Pacific Division. The 30-year-old posted his eighth career five-point performance in a 6-5 shootout win over the Carolina Hurricanes on Thursday and enters the week riding a six-game goal streak. Cooley stopped 66 of 68 shots across two starts to post a 1.00 goals-against average and .971 save percentage while helping the Flames extend their winning streak to three games. Fowler went 2-0-0 with a 1.00 goals-against average last week. items.body: Winning is becoming a way of life for the Carolina Hurricanes . The Canes, of course, captured the Stanley Cup about four months ago, validating several seasons of high-end hockey with that elusive title. If you thought Carolina might be slowed by a championship hangover — a guilty hand is going up right here — think again. The Storm Boys walloped the St. Louis Blues 4-0 in Missouri on Saturday and sit comfortably atop a Metropolitan Division that got a bit tougher over the weekend (more on that later). Even without a game on Sunday, the Hurricanes still scored a ‘W’ by inking 25-year-old defenceman Alexander Nikishin — a restricted free agent who had not played this season — to a one-year deal worth $3 million. Considering Nikishin’s ask was thought to be somewhere in the Zeev Buium range — the young Canucks blue-liner signed an extension worth $75 over eight years in early September — it’s easy to see this one-year pact as a coup for Canes GM Eric Tulsky and his front office. Now, if you want to look at this through a different lens, it’s fair to wonder if the optimal outcome with Nikishin was to make him part of a package to acquire goalie Connor Hellebuyck from Winnipeg. This week runs Monday, Oct. 26 to Sunday, Nov. 1, with 47 games on the schedule. Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday are all light nights with five or fewer games, so those are the nights to target if you have an open roster spot. Tuesday and Thursday are the busiest nights of the week with 11 games each, and Saturday isn’t far behind with 10, which means streamers will have a tough time cracking your lineup on all three nights. The Edmonton Oilers lead the way with 4.19 True Games, followed by the Calgary Flames , Toronto Maple Leafs , Los Angeles Kings and Ottawa Senators . At the other end, the Pittsburgh Penguins have the toughest week for streamers at just 1.41 True Games. In competitive leagues, you’re probably not finding Nugent-Hopkins on the waiver wire, but I was surprised to see he’s still available in 41 percent of leagues. Since returning to the lineup, RNH has recorded one goal, one assist and five SOG. More importantly, he’s fired 11 shot attempts while averaging 19:57 TOI/GP. That’s a level of shot volume we’ve rarely seen from Nugent-Hopkins, and while it’s unlikely to continue at that pace, it’s certainly encouraging. items.body: Defenseman began career with Canucks before trade to Minnesota last season VANCOUVER -- Quinn Hughes heard a lot of boos in his first game back in Vancouver, but a mixture of cheers during a first period tribute video is how the Minnesota Wild defenseman will remember an emotional night. Hughes was booed steadily from the time he first stepped on the ice for warmups, when he was shown on the scoreboard during the national anthems, and every time he touched the puck in a 4-2 Minnesota win against the Vancouver Canucks on Sunday. But the booing turned to a mix of cheers and some standing ovations during the video tribute, and it did not go unnoticed. "I was just proud," said Hughes, who skated out from the Wild bench and saluted the crowd with a raised stick. "And obviously I was here for six-and-a-half years, tried my best. And got some cheers there. That was cool for me." Hughes scored on the power play at 12:55 of the second period to put the Wild ahead 3-0 for his 500th point in his 520th game, making him the seventh fastest defenseman all-time -- and second fastest American defenseman after Brian Leetch (496 games) -- to reach the milestone. He added an assist by sending Kirill Kaprizov in on a breakaway for his NHL-leading 13th goal of the season to make it 4-0 at 3:38 of the third period to make it 501 points (69 goals, 432 assists). "I wasn't thinking about it like that," he said of the milestone. "I just wanted to get a win … and then I think just seeing the fans and being able to play here again was pretty cool for me. But as far as 500 points, where that happened, it happened." items.body: VANCOUVER — Quinn Hughes had listened to about 33 minutes of near-constant boos and jeers. The Montreal Canadiens goalie soaked up as much of the atmosphere as he could in the 2-1 win against the Winnipeg Jets, becoming the youngest goalie to play and win an NHL outdoor game. “This game was different than a lot of other games I played where a lot of times, you’re looking at the clock kind of waiting for it to run out,” Fowler said. “Obviously you want to get the win, but I think tonight was one of those games where you never want the game to end. “It’s so fun to be out there. The two of us (defenseman Lane Hutson ) we’ve been talking about it. We wish we can play more of these. It’s so fun, it’s such a great environment, the ice was pretty good, so it’s just a lot of fun, I definitely took in my fair share of the moment there.” Fowler made 33 saves in the win, earning first star honors. At 21 years and 355 days, he was the youngest goalie in the history of the NHL to start an outdoor game. This was the 21-year-old’s biggest game of the 23 he’s played in this league to date. items.body: VANCOUVER — A chorus of boos echoed through Rogers Arena as Quinn Hughes stepped on the ice for warm-ups on Sunday. The former Vancouver Canucks captain was back inside the rink for the first time since being traded to the Minnesota Wild in December, and some fans vocally displayed their displeasure with the move. Hundreds of people — many clad in Canucks jerseys emblazoned with Hughes' name and No. 43 — stood around the glass ahead of warm-ups, hoping to get a glimpse of the star defenceman. One held a sign reading "And I thought I had commitment issues." Hughes came into Sunday's game knowing a frosty reception was possible. "I don’t know what to expect too much (on Sunday) but we’ll face that when it comes," he said Saturday. Fans booed once again as a tribute to the blue liner began on the big screen during the first TV timeout, transformed into a mixed review, with whistles and clapping, and some in the crowd standing in ovation. The Stars have 20 straight penalty kills through its last five games, three on Sunday. The game was Dallas’ third in a six-game homestand and began a three-game Central Division trip for New York. items.summary: Alexander Nikishin signed a one-year, $3 million contract with the Carolina Hurricanes on Sunday.
items.body: Defenseman was restricted free agent, helped Carolina win Stanley Cup as rookie Alexander Nikishin signed a one-year, $3 million contract with the Carolina Hurricanes on Sunday. The 25-year-old defenseman has yet to play this season. He became a restricted free agent July 1 after he had 33 points (11 goals, 22 assists) and averaged 18:11 of ice time in 81 regular-season games as a rookie last season. His 11 goals set a Carolina/Hartford Whalers record for a rookie at his position ahead of Justin Faulk 's eight in 66 games of the 2011-12 season and his 33 points were second to Brad Shaw's 35 for the Whalers in 1989-90. "We're glad that Alexander is returning to our group," Hurricanes general manager Eric Tulsky said. "This has been a long process, but we look forward to him re-entering our locker room ready to contribute with the Hurricanes, as he did during a Stanley Cup championship season last year." Nikishin, named to the 2025-26 NHL All-Rookie Team, had one assist in 17 Stanley Cup Playoff games to help the Hurricanes win their first championship since 2006. A third-round pick (No. 69) by Carolina in the 2020 NHL Draft, Nikishin made his NHL debut on May 15, 2025, playing 10:33 in a 3-1 win against the Washington Capitals in Game 5 of the Eastern Conference Second Round that sent the Hurricanes to the Eastern Conference Final. Carolina (9-2-2) leads the NHL with 20 points and hosts the Boston Bruins at Lenovo Center on Tuesday (8 p.m. ET; ESPN, SN360).

His premium linemates contribute to the offensive luck that Roslovic has been having, with his aggressive mentality averaging just under three shots on goal per game. Reimer had signed a professional tryout agreement with the Rangers' AHL affiliate, the Hartford Wolf Pack, 10 days ago. In the 16 seasons that followed, he played in 539 regular-season games. He compiled a record of 232-191-67, with a GAA of 2.87 and a save percentage of .909. A fourth-round pick in the 2006 NHL Draft, Reimer spent his first eight seasons in the pros with the Toronto Maple Leafs organization. He then played for the Florida Panthers, Carolina Hurricanes, San Jose Sharks, Detroit Red Wings, Anaheim Ducks and Buffalo Sabres before joining the Senators. items.body: WINNIPEG — Outdoor hockey in Winnipeg, mercifully in October rather than December or January. “I’m thankful for that,” said Montreal Canadiens defenceman Kaiden Guhle, who recalls days from his youth that proved too cold for lake hockey behind his house in Edmonton. Sunday’s Heritage Classic against the Winnipeg Jets (Sportsnet, Sportsnet+, 7 p.m. ET / 6 p.m. CT) will be Guhle’s first NHL open-air experience, and despite the uniqueness of playing under the bright lights, and in front of more than 30,000 fans expected at Princess Auto Stadium, it’ll be a callback to when he first fell in love with the game, to when it was about nothing more than fun with friends. Only this time, no extra layers will be required, with the forecast calling for clear skies and a temperature of 3 C at puck drop. “That’s perfect,” said Oliver Kapanen, who played outdoor hockey every day after school in Timra, Finland, but has also never experienced anything like what he’ll live through on Sunday. Chris Kreider already has done it several times, so you can excuse him for not being as enthusiastic about it. “It’s only enjoyable if you win,” said the 35-year-old, who has a 3-0 record in outdoor NHL games but was on the wrong side of one in college, in his hometown, at Fenway Park, where he was first in awe of stepping foot in the Boston Red Sox room and then ultimately miserable sitting there after a loss. “It’s a dog and pony show, and if you lose it’s even more of a letdown,” Kreider added. “Two points, important to win a hockey game.” Phil Danault would love nothing more than for his Canadiens to beat the Jets after he lost with them to the Ottawa Senators in the NHL 100 Classic in 2017 at TD Place. “I lost another 6-1 to Minnesota when I was in my second season with Chicago, too,” said Danau

items.title: Who are the best Canadian goaltenders right now?
items.summary: Jordan Binnington led the way for Canada’s men’s team at the 2026 Winter Olympics. Will someone else step up down the road?
items.body: Add to Preferred Sources Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect If you were asked who the best Canadian goaltenders were a dozen or so games into the 2026-27 NHL regular season, which names would come to mind? You might go straight to the Washington Capitals’ Logan Thompson, or the Colorado Avalanche’s Mackenzie Blackwood. There’s even one goalie for the St. Louis Blues who has stood out, but it may not be the one you think… On Tuesday’s episode of Daily Faceoff LIVE , former NHL goaltender Carter Hutton and former NHL video coach Steve Peters take part in another edition of the #AskDFO segment, where they try to determine who is Canada’s top goalie so far in 2026-27. Carter Hutton : I’ll let you go first since you have seniority: who do you think is Canada’s hope right now, as Jordan Binnington has been on the outside looking in. Steve Peters : I think if we had to go today, I’d go with Logan Thompson. He’s a more experienced guy, he’s had success in the last few years … I think he gives me the warm fuzzies. If he’s in the net, he gives me some security. Jordan Binnington, he’s a guy who even if he struggles, has been outstanding for Team Canada. But I do think it’s time to pass the torch, and for me, that guy is Logan Thompson. Carter Hutton : This is where I think this situation gets very interesting, because of the depth situation we have, right? You think about the particular names we’ve heard: Mackenzie Blackwood, Jordan Binnington, Darcy Kuemper, Adin Hill … I think you take all those guys out of the list. As a No. 3, Binnington could stay, just based on experience in a sort of “break glass in case of emergency” situation. But for me, it’s the young guys: Jet Greaves, Devon Levi, Joel Hofer. That’s a pretty good wave of guys coming. I think Thompson is your guy

items.title: Sunday Overreactions: Can Blue Jackets convince Werenski to stay?
items.summary: After Zach Werenski seemingly had a foot out the door in Columbus this summer, could the Blue Jackets’ slow start have trade talks pick up around the defenceman once again? Michael Amato dives into Werenski’s future and more in his Sunday Overreactions.
items.body: If the goal for the Columbus Blue Jackets this season was to quiet the noise from the summer, it isn’t going well. Head coach Rick Bowness was none too pleased during training camp with the conditioning of a couple of players. Then, he went off on his team after it gave up a touchdown to the Florida Panthers last week. Kirill Marchenko’s return on Tuesday was supposed to bring out the best in the Blue Jackets, but a 6-2 defeat was all they could muster. Even with Saturday night’s desperately needed win over the Vegas Golden Knights, the Blue Jackets still sit last in the Eastern Conference, having accumulated just eight points in nine games. Columbus's problems are deeper than the standings, though. Marchenko didn’t hide the fact that he wanted out, and for a moment, it felt like Zach Werenski had one foot out the door this summer, as well. General manager Don Waddell and Werenski smoothed things over, but it may only have been a temporary reprieve. The reigning Norris Trophy winner’s contract doesn’t expire until the summer of 2028. But as we know, teams like to have clarity on their best players' intentions much earlier than that. That means the clock is ticking on Werenski, who is eligible to sign an extension next summer. We saw what the Vancouver Canucks did with Quinn Hughes and the Ottawa Senators with Brady Tkachuk, when it became clear both had no interest in re-signing. You could argue the Blue Jackets may even be in a more urgent state than the Canucks and Senators. Werenski at least thought seriously enough about moving on in the summer that Waddell was exploring trade options, before the two ultimately released a statement that reaffirmed Werenski’s commitment to the team.
